title: Develop and implement an extension programme plan

lessons.title: Situation analysis and needs assessment
lessons.html:
Start with the situation, not the solution

An extension programme plan is a written plan that sets out what an extension service will do, for whom, why, how, when and with what resources. A good plan starts by understanding the situation of the clients before choosing activities.

Situation analysis

Collect information about the area and the target group:

  • Natural resources: rainfall, soils, veld condition, water sources, climate risks such as drought or hail.
  • Farming systems: main crops and livestock, scale, methods, yields and production problems.
  • People: number of farmers, gender and age mix, literacy, household labour, organisations and leadership.
  • Economic factors: access to inputs, credit, markets, transport and prices.
  • Institutions: other programmes and role players already active in the area.

Use existing reports and statistics, transect walks, community meetings, participatory mapping and individual interviews.

Identifying and ranking needs

Distinguish between needs felt by farmers and needs observed by technical experts. For example, farmers may name lack of a tractor as the main problem, while you observe that low soil fertility and late planting cause most yield loss. Both matter. Discuss them openly with the community and agree on priorities together.

A simple tool is pairwise ranking, where the group compares problems two at a time and votes on which is more important. Another is a problem tree, which separates the core problem from its causes and its effects. For instance, a core problem of low calving rates in a communal herd may have causes such as poor winter nutrition, uncontrolled breeding, and disease, with effects such as low income and fewer animals to sell.

From needs to programme focus

Choose a focus that is important to farmers, technically sound, achievable with available resources and within your mandate. A narrow, well-supported programme achieves more than a wide plan that tries to solve everything at once.

lessons.title: Writing the programme plan
lessons.html:
Elements of a programme plan

1. Goal and objectives

The goal is the broad long-term change, for example improved household income from cattle in the ward. Objectives are specific, measurable, achievable, relevant and time-bound (SMART). Example: by March next year, 30 members of the livestock association will have introduced a controlled breeding season.

2. Target group

State who the programme is for, how many people and selection criteria.

3. Activities and methods

List the activities needed for each objective, with methods suited to the audience: group training, demonstrations, farmer field schools, individual visits, exchange visits and information days.

4. Work plan

ActivityWhenWhoResources
Bull selection workshopSeptemberExtension officer, animal health technicianVenue, transport, handouts
Fence repair for bull campOctoberAssociation membersWire, droppers, labour
Pregnancy diagnosis dayAprilPrivate vet, extension officerCrush pen, vet fees

Match timing to the farming calendar. Do not schedule training during planting or harvest.

5. Budget

Estimate costs in rands: transport, venues, materials, catering, demonstration inputs, specialist fees. Show what will come from your organisation, partners and farmers themselves.

6. Roles and partners

Name responsible people and partner organisations, and confirm their commitment before finalising the plan.

7. Monitoring and evaluation

Define indicators, baseline, data collection methods and reporting dates.

8. Risks

List risks such as drought, input delays, disease outbreaks or loss of key staff, and how you will respond.

Present the draft plan to farmers and your supervisor for comment and approval before implementation. A plan farmers helped to write is one they are more likely to support.

lessons.title: Implementing and adjusting the plan
lessons.html:
From paper to practice

Implementation is where most programmes succeed or fail. Good preparation, coordination and follow-up make the difference.

Preparing each activity

  • Confirm dates, venue and facilitators at least a week ahead.
  • Notify farmers through the channels they actually use: WhatsApp groups, the induna, church announcements, the dip tank committee.
  • Prepare materials in the local language and test demonstrations beforehand.
  • Check safety arrangements, for example a strong crush pen for cattle handling, protective equipment for spraying demonstrations, and a first aid kit.

Running activities

Start on time, keep an attendance register, involve farmers actively and finish with agreed actions. After each activity, write a short activity report: what was done, who attended, problems and follow-up needed.

Coordinating partners

Hold regular short meetings or calls with partners to review progress. Share the work plan so everyone knows what is coming. When a partner changes plans, update the schedule and inform farmers quickly.

Monitoring progress

Compare actual progress with the work plan each month. Track activities completed, attendance, inputs delivered, money spent against budget and early signs of change on farms. A simple progress table with green, amber and red ratings helps you and your supervisor see problems early.

Adjusting the plan

Plans must respond to reality. If a drought delays planting, move crop demonstrations and bring forward fodder and water topics. If farmers show strong interest in a related topic, consider adding it if resources allow. Record every significant change, the reason for it and who approved it.

Closing the programme cycle

At the end of the cycle, evaluate results against objectives, report to stakeholders and use lessons learned to design the next plan.

Key points

  • Base the plan on a situation analysis and agreed priority needs.
  • Write SMART objectives and link every activity to an objective.
  • Include a work plan, budget, roles, monitoring and risks.
  • Prepare activities carefully, including safety arrangements.
  • Monitor monthly and adjust the plan with documented reasons.
